reference.source: Braddom's Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation / pain medicine references
clinicalPearls: Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone with exaggerated tendon reflexes, arising as part of the upper motor neuron syndrome after brain or spinal cord injury
It should be assessed for its functional impact using scales such as the Modified Ashworth Scale, since not all spasticity is harmful and some may aid standing or transfers
A key first step is to identify and remove noxious triggers such as infection, pressure injury, constipation, urinary retention, ingrown nails, or poor positioning that can suddenly worsen tone
Management follows a stepped approach beginning with therapy and physical measures: stretching, positioning, splinting, serial casting, and an appropriate seating and standing programme
Focal spasticity affecting a few muscles is well suited to intramuscular botulinum toxin injection to reduce tone in targeted muscles and enable therapy
Generalised spasticity may require oral agents such as baclofen, tizanidine, dantrolene, or benzodiazepines, weighing benefit against sedation and weakness
Severe, diffuse spasticity refractory to oral treatment may be managed with intrathecal baclofen delivered by an implanted pump
Treatment goals should be explicit and functional, whether to improve mobility, ease care and hygiene, relieve pain, or prevent contracture, and outcomes reassessed regularly
Untreated spasticity can lead to fixed contractures, pain, pressure injury, and impaired hygiene, so proactive management is important
reference.pathophysiology: Spasticity results from loss of descending inhibitory control over spinal reflex circuits following upper motor neuron lesions. Reduced supraspinal inhibition leads to hyperexcitability of the stretch reflex arc, with increased alpha motor neuron excitability, altered interneuronal modulation, and diminished presynaptic and reciprocal inhibition. Over time, secondary changes within muscle and connective tissue, including altered viscoelastic properties and contracture, add a non-neural component to the increased resistance felt on passive movement.
additionalDifferentials: Rigidity of parkinsonian or extrapyramidal origin
Rigidity from neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Structured tone assessment using the Modified Ashworth or Tardieu scale
Evaluation for noxious triggers including urinalysis, review of bowel and bladder function, and skin inspection
Goal-setting assessment and gait or functional analysis to guide treatment targets
Dynamic assessment with diagnostic nerve or motor point blocks to distinguish dynamic spasticity from fixed contracture
Imaging or electrophysiology where an evolving or new central lesion is suspected
redFlags: A sudden, unexplained increase in tone that may signal infection, pressure injury, fracture, or another noxious stimulus
New or rapidly progressive spasticity suggesting an evolving spinal cord or intracranial lesion such as syringomyelia
Signs of intrathecal baclofen withdrawal, which can be life-threatening with high fever, rebound spasticity, and rhabdomyolysis
Developing pressure injury or contracture threatening skin integrity and function
reference.prognosis: With individualised, goal-directed treatment most patients achieve meaningful reductions in tone, pain, and care burden, though spasticity in progressive neurological disease may continue to evolve. Early and consistent management reduces the risk of irreversible contracture and secondary complications.
pitfalls: Treating spasticity aggressively when it is actually providing useful functional support for standing or transfers
Failing to look for and remove a noxious trigger before escalating drug therapy
Over-sedating patients with oral agents, causing weakness and functional decline
Missing intrathecal baclofen pump malfunction or abrupt withdrawal
Neglecting stretching, positioning, and therapy while relying solely on medication
management: Identify and remove noxious triggers such as infection, urinary retention, constipation, pressure injury, ingrown nails or poor positioning that aggravate tone
First-line physical measures: stretching, positioning, splinting, serial casting and a structured seating and standing programme
Intramuscular botulinum toxin for focal spasticity to reduce tone in targeted muscles and enable therapy
Oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen, tizanidine, dantrolene or benzodiazepines for generalised spasticity, balancing benefit against sedation and weakness
Intrathecal baclofen for severe generalised spasticity refractory to oral therapy
Set functional, goal-directed targets and assess tone with validated scales, treating only spasticity that impairs function
Multidisciplinary rehabilitation input, with orthopaedic or neurosurgical referral (for example selective dorsal rhizotomy) for fixed deformity or refractory disease
